theory.intro: When a ratio is given together with the value of **one** of its quantities, find the value of **one part** first. Once one part is known you can multiply to reach whatever the question wants — the other quantity, the total, or the gap between them. This is the **unitary method**.
facts: In the ratio $m:n$ the two quantities are made of $m$ parts and $n$ parts, and every part is worth the same.
Divide the given amount by its number of parts to find $1$ part: if $3\text{ parts}=12$ L then $1\text{ part}=4$ L.
The total is $m+n$ parts and the gap between the two quantities is $m-n$ parts.
A part value need not be a whole number — $4\text{ parts}=10$ L gives $1\text{ part}=2.5$ L.
A bar model shows the parts as equal cells, one bar per quantity, with the known amount marked against its own bar.
steps: Identify the number of parts the given quantity represents.
Divide to find the value of $1$ part.
Multiply to find the required number of parts.

development.question_text: Faith makes orange paint by mixing $12$ litres of red paint with $15$ litres of yellow paint. She wants more of exactly the same shade and uses another $8$ litres of yellow paint. How many more litres of red paint does she need?
development.solution_text:
$12:15$
$=4:5$
$5\text{ parts}=8\text{ L}$
$1\text{ part}=1.6\text{ L}$
$4\text{ parts}=6.4\text{ L of red paint}$

mastery.question_text: A shortbread recipe uses flour and butter in the ratio $9:2$. Ben has $1000$ g of flour and $200$ g of butter, and he uses all of the butter. How much flour is left over?
mastery.solution_text:
$2\text{ parts}=200\text{ g}$
$1\text{ part}=100\text{ g}$
$9\text{ parts}=900\text{ g of flour used}$
$1000-900=100\text{ g left over}$

mastery.question_text: At a swimming club the ratio of juniors to seniors is $7:2$. There are $12$ seniors. Some juniors then leave and the ratio becomes $2:1$, with the number of seniors unchanged. How many juniors left?
mastery.solution_text:
$2\text{ parts}=12$
$1\text{ part}=6$
$7\text{ parts}=42\text{ juniors at first}$
$1\text{ new part}=12$
$2\text{ new parts}=24\text{ juniors now}$
$42-24=18\text{ juniors left}$

mastery.question_text: Rectangle $A$ has its width and length in the ratio $2:5$ and its width is $6$ cm. Rectangle $B$ has its width and length in the ratio $3:4$ and its length is $20$ cm. Which rectangle has the greater perimeter, and by how much?
mastery.solution_text:
$2\text{ parts}=6\text{ cm}$
$1\text{ part}=3\text{ cm}$
$5\text{ parts}=15\text{ cm}$
$P_A=2\times(6+15)=42\text{ cm}$
$4\text{ parts}=20\text{ cm}$
$1\text{ part}=5\text{ cm}$
$3\text{ parts}=15\text{ cm}$
$P_B=2\times(15+20)=70\text{ cm}$
Rectangle $B$ is greater, by $70-42=28$ cm.
